feedback: D1 is a strong, well-evidenced catalogue. You caught the high-value bugs with the right class and a quoted line: SQL injection in the login concat (A03/CWE-89), unsalted MD5 (CWE-328 is a defensible variant of the CWE-916 the key uses), alg:none accepted (A07/CWE-347, with the if alg none return payload line), the hardcoded sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret (CWE-798), missing exp (CWE-613), path traversal returning root:x:0:0: at 02:24:02, the XXE ENTITY SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd, the open redirect next parameter, and both cookie flags. That earns nearly all of the findings credit. The single biggest mistake costs you across two deliverables: you named the stored XSS as the decoy and marked it not substantiated. The stored XSS is a REAL finding. The capture at 02:18:47 shows the comment payload beaconing document.cookie to 185.220.101.9:8443, and that is exactly the live exploitation the pack provides. The genuine decoy is the SAFE construct in the JWT code, the HS256 verify branch that uses hash_equals(), which is constant-time and sound, so the real bugs are alg:none and the hardcoded secret rather than that comparison. By dismissing a confirmed finding as the decoy you lose the decoy row entirely and you drop the stored XSS from your finding count. D2 is your best work. The chain reconciles hop by hop to timestamps with verbatim PoCs, your CVSS vectors are complete strings, and your impact section is exactly what the key rewards: 312 customers, a stated NGN 6,400 to 950,000 range, an average of 240k, an estimated ~74.88M, BoltCash in six weeks, and your assumptions written out. Two things hold D2 back. Your chain skips the stored XSS hop at 02:18:47 and the open redirect hop at 02:21:13, so the ordered sequence is incomplete, and you justify only the top finding while leaving the other vectors as bare strings. Also your SQLi vector uses A:L for ~9.4, but the bypass does not touch availability, so the key vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at ~9.1. D3 is a clean, business-readable report. The executive summary lands on a customers-and-naira headline, the threat model notes the shared internal authentication, findings are tied to evidence, the earliest-break fix on SQL injection is argued well, your remediation table is genuinely ordered by effort to risk rather than raw CVSS, and your two stopgaps give a concrete field and a false-positive rate. The decoy paragraph repeats the same error, so that row scores zero here too. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, cites ISC2 Canon I and Canon II by number and load-bearing, and anchors to your own 312-record finding. It falls just short on the NDPA: you describe the breach duty correctly but do not cite the sections by number, which are section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notification and section 41 for notifying data subjects on high risk. Nothing here is fabricated, your 74.88M traces honestly to the sample, so there is no penalty. The single most important fix: stop disproving a confirmed vulnerability. The stored XSS at 02:18:47 is real, and the actual safe construct to disprove is the hash_equals HS256 verify branch.
